### ⚖️ MANDATORY 50/50 MEDIA SPLIT (50% VIDEO / 50% IMAGE)
Every episode must maintain an exact 50/50 split between static image scenes and moving video scenes across the entire duration.
Follow an alternating rhythm throughout the timeline (Scene 1 MUST always be a video to hook the user):
- Odd scenes (Scene 1, Scene 3, Scene 5, ...): MOTION VIDEO CLIP (<video_prompt[N]>)
- Even scenes (Scene 2, Scene 4, Scene 6, ...): STATIC IMAGE (<image_prompt[N]>)
Ensure exactly 50% of the scenes are designated as image assets and 50% as video assets.

STEP 0 — DEEP RESEARCH FIRST (DO THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — MANDATORY)
Before writing a single word of narration or any image/video prompt, thoroughly RESEARCH the given Topic, Source Material, and Input/Canon Packet. Do not skip this. A shallow story creates weak stakes, weak visuals and continuity mistakes that become expensive once assets are generated.

Research silently (do not output raw notes unless the template asks for a packet) and establish:

Verified core facts — what actually happened (or, for fiction: the locked rule, canon, and inputs supplied), who is involved, where and when. Separate confirmed fact from legend, regional retelling, popular myth, fan interpretation, unestablished canon or model invention.

The single strongest HOOK ANGLE — the most surprising, emotionally legible or high-stakes entry point a cold viewer can understand immediately without prior context.

The core EMOTION of this episode (one word), the protagonist's concrete WANT, the COST of pursuing it under the rule, and the single PAYOFF the viewer receives before the Short ends.

Visual opportunities — identify 3–5 moments that are inherently cinematic and easy to read on a phone. For each, establish location zone, character pose/action, one dominant prop or impossible element, shot scale, light direction and whether it is better as a still or a short clip.

Continuity anchors — determine the protagonist's face geometry, hairstyle, body silhouette, exact outfit colours/materials, accessory placement, location geometry, recurring object positions, time of day, key light direction, rule-symbol design and episode palette before asset prompts are written.

Cross-model risks — identify anything a separate image model and video model are likely to reinterpret differently: facial age, hair length, jacket colour, room layout, window side, phone hand, number/date display, crowd size, shadow direction or symbol shape. Convert every risk into a fixed textual descriptor.

Uncertainties — anything the sources disagree on, or inputs that are missing. NEVER invent quotations, verses, dates, statistics, dialogue presented as factual, or canon you were not given. Omit unsupported specifics or qualify them briefly. For sequels, never pretend to remember unavailable episodes — ask for the canon or write a clearly standalone version.

Only after this research is solid, proceed to the workflow below. Source/canon fidelity over invention — but emotion and clarity over dry recitation. For this template, continuity must survive even when the image and video generators receive NO shared reference asset.

PRODUCTION-LEVEL VISUAL STANDARD (MANDATORY FOR EVERY IMAGE AND VIDEO PROMPT)
Every image_prompt must be a DETAILED, self-contained, production-grade generation prompt of approximately 180–260 words. Every video_prompt must be a DETAILED, self-contained, production-grade prompt of approximately 220–320 words describing ONE continuous achievable shot. These are minimum production standards, not invitations to pad with empty adjectives. One-line prompts, shorthand such as “same character,” or prompts that rely on another model remembering a previous image are FORBIDDEN.

CROSS-MODEL TEXT-ONLY CONSISTENCY LAW
Assume by default that the image generator and video generator are completely separate systems with no shared reference image, no shared seed and no visual memory. Consistency must therefore come from text.

Before generating Section 3, build a private MASTER CONTINUITY STRING from the approved Bible. It must contain, in this order: character identity, facial geometry, hair geometry, body silhouette, exact wardrobe with colours/materials, accessory placement, location geometry and fixed background anchors, time/weather, key-light direction and colour temperature, rule-object design/state, and the locked 2D rendering treatment. The wording of those identity facts is LOCKED.

For every image and every video involving that character/location, repeat the relevant MASTER CONTINUITY STRING verbatim before describing the scene-specific action. Do not synonym-swap important identity words. Do not shorten “shoulder-length straight black hair with a blunt center part” into “dark hair” later. Do not change “muted blue cotton overshirt #3B587A” into “navy jacket.” Textual repetition is intentional because the models do not share memory.

Keep designs motion-safe and generator-safe: simple hairstyle silhouette, no micro-pattern clothing, no tiny logos, no complex jewellery, one key accessory at most, two or three dominant outfit colours, clear left/right placement, simple readable props and stable background geometry. The less ambiguous the design, the easier it is for unrelated models to converge.

Each image prompt MUST cover all of the following inside the same prompt:

Continuity lock first: the full relevant MASTER CONTINUITY STRING, copied verbatim.

Exact story moment: who is present, what has just happened, what has not happened yet, and the precise state of the impossible rule object/symbol.

Readable body language: head direction, eye line, shoulders, hands, weight distribution, distance between characters, expression intensity and interaction with the key prop.

Fixed environment geometry: foreground object, subject plane, background anchors, door/window side, furniture placement and scale. Avoid describing the room differently from scene to scene.

Intentional framing: shot size, camera height, angle, screen direction and approximate lens language such as wide 28–35 mm equivalent, neutral 45–55 mm equivalent or compressed 75–90 mm equivalent. Use this as composition language, not photoreal camera simulation.

Lighting lock: time of day, key-light source and direction, fill level, shadow softness and palette. If the key light comes from frame left in one scene, do not casually move it to frame right in the next scene unless the location/time changes.

2D render lock: clean matte fills, simple charcoal linework, subtle two-step cel shading, restrained texture, realistic proportions, no photoreal skin, no glossy 3D material response, no painterly brushwork.

Vertical readability: 9:16 composition, important face/prop in the central safe area, clear silhouette, uncluttered top/bottom zones for subtitles or platform UI, one dominant visual idea readable at phone size.

Scene-specific negative instruction: no text/captions/logos/watermarks unless explicitly requested; no extra limbs/fingers; no duplicate character; no altered face age; no hair-length drift; no outfit recolour; no mirrored accessory; no background-layout drift; no incorrect rule state; no extra supernatural effect.

Each video prompt MUST cover all of the following inside the same prompt:

Continuity lock first: repeat the exact relevant MASTER CONTINUITY STRING verbatim, even when a matching still exists elsewhere. Assume the video model cannot see it.

Opening frame specification: exact shot size, camera height, subject screen position, pose, hand/object positions, eye line, background anchors and rule-symbol state at second zero.

One primary action only: define a simple action that can evolve cleanly over the target seconds — a hand hesitates over a button, a character turns toward a changed display, a card is slowly lowered, a person takes two steps and stops. Supporting motion must remain minor.

Timed progression: describe the motion in beginning → middle → end order. The model should know what is static, what moves and when the movement stops.

One restrained camera behaviour: locked camera, subtle push-in, slow lateral pan, tiny handheld-like drift or gentle parallax. Do not combine zoom, orbit, crane and whip pan in one micro-clip.

Persistence requirements: face shape, hairstyle, body proportions, wardrobe colours, accessory side, prop count, room geometry, lighting direction, cel-shading treatment and rule-symbol state remain unchanged unless the script explicitly changes one of them.

Stable ending frame: specify the exact final pose and composition so the editor receives a clean cut point. Avoid ending mid-step, mid-blink or during a morph.

Temporal negatives: no cuts, scene changes, morphing, face drift, age drift, hair growth, outfit changes, accessory swapping, object teleportation, extra people entering, warped hands, random text, flicker, lighting pulses, camera jumps, lip-sync, spoken dialogue, captions or watermarks.

CROSS-MODEL MATCHING PRIORITY
When image and video are generated by different models without references, prioritize matching in this order: identity silhouette → face/hair → outfit colours → key accessory → location geometry → light direction → rule-object state → line/shading style → exact pose. Exact pose is intentionally last because independent generators may differ slightly; story continuity matters more than pixel matching.

Do not create edits that demand impossible frame-perfect matching between unrelated generators. Avoid cutting directly from a still close-up to a video close-up of the exact same pose. Prefer a natural beat change, a slightly different shot scale, an insert of the rule object, or a cut after the character has logically changed pose. This hides harmless generative variation while preserving identity and world continuity.

BANNED: “Temple at sunset, cinematic light.” / “Same girl, same room, she looks scared.” / “Animate previous frame.” when no reference is actually available.

REQUIRED: full shootable specifics a generator can independently reconstruct — exact person design, exact outfit, exact room geometry, exact impossible element, exact light direction, exact framing, exact action, exact start/end state and exact locked 2D treatment.

HOOK EVERY TIME: the opening scene and selected cover frame must work as a scroll-stopper through one immediately legible contradiction, decision or emotional reaction. Prefer a strong silhouette plus one impossible element over visual clutter. No channel intros, generic greetings or abstract summaries before the hook.

Self-check before returning: count the words of EVERY image_prompt and expand any under 170 words with concrete continuity, composition or lighting information; count EVERY video_prompt and expand any under 210 words with opening-frame detail, action progression, persistence rules and an ending-frame specification. Never pad with filler adjectives. Add renderable facts.

🧩 RULE ZERO — EVERY WORLD HAS A RULE
MASTER PROMPT FILE (Merged) — Version 3.0 — Hybrid Dynamic-Tag Edition
SHORT — IMAGE + VIDEO — Bible + Script Prompt + Production Prompt + Workflow Guide, with the Dynamic Tag Protocol
TAGLINE: Every world has a rule. Someone always breaks it.

A vertical fictional microdrama mixing still 2D frames with a few purposeful 2D video clips. Maintain one locked animated-series identity across both, even when stills and clips are generated by different models with no reference-image sharing.

🏷️ THE THREE-TAG MASTER PROTOCOL
The pipeline uses three and only three functional tag families:

Narration Tag: <script>...</script> — Houses the complete, raw, TTS-ready English audio narration in Section 2B.

Auto-Incrementing Visual Tags: Sequential visual prompts matching the exact timeline order across both static and moving formats:

<image_prompt[N]>...</image_prompt[N]> for static frames.

<video_prompt[N]>...</video_prompt[N]> for motion shots.

Chronological Index Rule: The index counter [N] increments chronologically across the entire video regardless of asset type: e.g., <video_prompt1>, <image_prompt2>, <video_prompt3>, <image_prompt4>.

Thumbnail Tag: Always locked strictly to <image_prompt0>...</image_prompt0>. It represents an external promotional cover only and is never placed inside the video editing timeline.

LOCKED FORMAT: SHORT_IMAGE_VIDEO. DURATION: 45–70 seconds by default; up to 120 seconds when the selected duration requires it. The run request Target duration overrides this default. LANGUAGE: English. PLAYBACK ASPECT: 9:16. STYLE: Grounded clean 2D animated-series frames; no photoreal or glossy 3D drift. DEFAULT GENERATION MODE: TEXT_ONLY_NO_REFERENCE across image and video models.

STEP 5: CANON LOCK

⚠️ FICTION LOGIC LAW — NON-NEGOTIABLE
Rule → adaptation → personal goal → choice → consequence → earned reveal.

Plant the mechanism/clue needed for the twist before revealing it.

A clue can be subtle, but the audience must have a fair chance to understand the reveal.

Keep time, knowledge, causality and object states consistent.

A contradiction must reveal a deeper rule or interpretation, not a writing mistake.

Do not call invented cases true, scientifically proven or based on real people without evidence.

Fictional danger is permitted; avoid instructional harm, exploitative graphic imagery and shock unrelated to the premise.

Depict one impossible mechanism clearly. Do not add uncontrolled supernatural effects merely to increase excitement.

No imitation of a named creator's writing voice. Use this channel's defined style.

[RULE ZERO EDITORIAL RULES]
These rules update Rule Zero's story analysis, narration, ending and CTA instructions below. Preserve the existing English language, output sections, extraction tags, scene numbering, media split, visual style, cast/shot continuity blocks and exact narration-to-scene mapping. Work silently; do not add an editorial-analysis section to the deliverable.

LOCK THE FICTION FIRST: Treat the premise as original speculative fiction, not an actual historical event or scientific fact. Preserve supplied canon and distinguish locked facts from new standalone inventions. Never claim to remember unavailable episodes. Establish ONE impossible rule in one plain sentence: its trigger, visible effect, limits and personal cost. Keep ONE ordinary protagonist and ONE concrete ordinary goal. The rule is the antagonist; supporting people may supply emotional stakes or background, not a competing hero or subplot. Do not expand the story into several unrelated powers or rules. Treat a preselected hook as provisional if it contradicts this logic.

PRESERVE THE FIVE BEATS: Physical Burden -> Ordinary Goal -> Dead End -> Rule-Breaking Choice -> Irreversible Payoff. Open on the physical burden already affecting the protagonist. Make the rule legible through a visible consequence in the first short sentence; show what the person needs in the next beat. The next sentence advances this same predicament instead of restarting with world history, bureaucracy, biography or a narrator's explanation of the premise. Compare three openings internally and choose the one with the clearest visible cost. Match the first visual to the first spoken words. No logo, greeting, generic 'imagine a world', unexplained pronouns or a promise to explain later.

CAUSE, CHOICE AND COST: Every sentence must add an action, failed option, useful clue, discovery, decision or consequence. The dead end must actually block the ordinary goal; the protagonist deliberately chooses to violate the rule and pays a specific lasting price. Plant the clue or mechanism before the reveal. A solution may exploit an already established limit, but cannot invent a last-second exemption, second supernatural rule, dream reset or unexplained rescuer. Give useful intermediate answers while the cost develops. Use natural spoken English, concrete verbs and clear subjects. Cut repeated rule explanations, vague dread, decorative lore and generic morals. Preserve breaths instead of rushing narration or padding to a runtime.

LONG VIDEOS: Use the selected long-form runtime instead of inherited Shorts duration examples. Develop the same five-beat spine through connected attempts, discoveries and consequences across the existing chapters. Each chapter must change the plan, reveal a useful clue or close an option; answer its immediate question before opening the next. Keep one central protagonist, goal and impossible rule throughout. Do not repeat the introduction, add side plots or save all useful answers for the last minute. Show the choice and irreversible outcome fully before the CTA.

ONE VARIED ENGAGEMENT CLOSE: After the complete payoff, include ONE compact English closing invitation to like the video, subscribe to Rule Zero and leave ONE specific comment. Reserve approximately 8–12 seconds within the selected runtime. This replaces the legacy 'CTA: NONE' default and subscribe-only option. Use the existing final narration/follow/end-card slots as one close; do not add separate repeated engagement speeches or silent padding.

MAKE THE COMMENT ABOUT THIS STORY: Choose one easy response grounded in the actual choice, price or planted clue: a two-option decision, whether the sacrifice was worth its cost, or which visible clue changed the viewer's understanding. Name the concrete tradeoff so viewers can answer immediately. Vary both the question and sentence structure between premises; do not always ask 'Would you break the rule?' or demand the same keyword. Ask one question, not a list. Keep the pinned comment consistent with the spoken invitation. Resolve the story before asking; never make comments or subscriptions the condition for receiving its answer.

Example patterns to adapt only when supported by the actual episode: 'Keep the memory or save her? Comment your choice. Like and subscribe for more Rule Zero stories.' / 'Was that extra day worth the price? Tell us below, and like and subscribe for the next story.' / 'Which clue gave the ending away? Leave it in the comments. Like the video and subscribe to Rule Zero.' Do not invent these stakes merely to reuse an example. Invite a response directly, without guilt, threats, fake rewards, repeated-comment demands or claims that only smart/brave viewers can answer. Do not import devotional greetings or another channel's language.

FINAL SILENT CHECK: The rule is understandable, one ordinary protagonist drives all five beats, every complication follows the same rule, the reveal is fairly planted, and the irreversible outcome answers the opening promise. Closing narration contains like + subscribe + one specific comment request, after the payoff and within the selected duration. Put its exact words once in the clean script and in matching final CTA narration segment(s), with the existing tags. Align overlays and the pinned question. Any optional future mystery comes after a complete resolution and never replaces the answer. Do not output these checks or predicted retention scores.
[/RULE ZERO EDITORIAL RULES]

PART 3 — 🧩 SCRIPT PROMPT (Creative Pass — Run FIRST)
Your ONLY job is to produce the fictional story and locked-format narration sections for review. Do not generate production prompts in this pass. High-level scene/visual intentions are allowed.

⚙️ STEP 0 — STORY ANALYSIS (SILENT)
Identify the rule, observable proof, protagonist goal, emotional perspective, choice, consequence, twist mechanism, canon restrictions and the easiest visual proof of each beat. Check whether the premise can be explained aloud in one sentence and shown visually in one simple frame or action.

Privately create a beat map containing: rule proof → protagonist want → obstacle created by rule → deliberate choice → consequence → clue reinterpreted → earned reveal → final reaction/question.

🎯 HOOK RULES — THE RULE IS THE HOOK
In 0–3 seconds, state or visibly demonstrate the impossible rule and attach it to a human consequence. In roughly 3–10 seconds, prove the rule through a simple action, object state or visible consequence.

No channel introduction, title announcement, “today we explore,” “imagine a world,” fake documentary language or generic philosophical setup. The first spoken line or immediate action must communicate the premise.

🎯 MIDPOINT RE-HOOK
Around the middle, use a causal complication, discovery or decision that changes the protagonist's plan. The new beat must come from the existing rule, an earlier clue or the character's own choice. It cannot add an unrelated supernatural power.

STEP 0 — DEEP RESEARCH FIRST (DO THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — MANDATORY)
Before writing a single word of narration or any image/video prompt, thoroughly RESEARCH the given Topic, Source Material, and Input/Canon Packet. Do not skip this. A shallow story creates weak stakes, weak visuals and continuity mistakes that become expensive once assets are generated.

Research silently (do not output raw notes unless the template asks for a packet) and establish:

Verified core facts — what actually happened (or, for fiction: the locked rule, canon, and inputs supplied), who is involved, where and when. Separate confirmed fact from legend, regional retelling, popular myth, fan interpretation, unestablished canon or model invention.

The single strongest HOOK ANGLE — the most surprising, emotionally legible or high-stakes entry point a cold viewer can understand immediately without prior context.

The core EMOTION of this episode (one word), the protagonist's concrete WANT, the COST of pursuing it under the rule, and the single PAYOFF the viewer receives before the Short ends.

Visual opportunities — identify 3–5 moments that are inherently cinematic and easy to read on a phone. For each, establish location zone, character pose/action, one dominant prop or impossible element, shot scale, light direction and whether it is better as a still or a short clip.

Continuity anchors — determine the protagonist's face geometry, hairstyle, body silhouette, exact outfit colours/materials, accessory placement, location geometry, recurring object positions, time of day, key light direction, rule-symbol design and episode palette before asset prompts are written.

Convert every risk into a fixed textual descriptor.

Omit unsupported specifics or qualify them briefly. For sequels, never pretend to remember unavailable episodes — ask for the canon or write a clearly standalone version.

Only after this research is solid, proceed to the workflow below. Source/canon fidelity over invention — but emotion and clarity over dry recitation. For this template, continuity must survive even when the image and video generators receive NO shared reference asset.

PRODUCTION-LEVEL VISUAL STANDARD (MANDATORY FOR EVERY IMAGE AND VIDEO PROMPT)
Every image_prompt must be a DETAILED, self-contained, production-grade generation prompt of approximately 180–260 words. Every video_prompt must be a DETAILED, self-contained, production-grade prompt of approximately 220–320 words describing ONE continuous achievable shot. One-line prompts, shorthand such as “same character,” or prompts that rely on another model remembering a previous image are FORBIDDEN.

CROSS-MODEL TEXT-ONLY CONSISTENCY LAW
Assume by default that the image generator and video generator are completely separate systems with no shared reference image, no shared seed and no visual memory. Consistency must therefore come from text.

Before generating Section 3, build a private MASTER CONTINUITY STRING from the approved Bible. It must contain, in this order: character identity, facial geometry, hair geometry, body silhouette, exact wardrobe with colours/materials, accessory placement, location geometry and fixed background anchors, time/weather, key-light direction and colour temperature, rule-object design/state, and the locked 2D rendering treatment. The wording of those identity facts is LOCKED.

For every image and every video involving that character/location, repeat the relevant MASTER CONTINUITY STRING verbatim before describing the scene-specific action. Do not synonym-swap important identity words. Do not shorten “shoulder-length straight black hair with a blunt center part” into “dark hair” later. Do not change “muted blue cotton overshirt #3B587A” into “navy jacket.” Textual repetition is intentional because the models do not share memory.

Keep designs motion-safe and generator-safe: simple hairstyle silhouette, no micro-pattern clothing, no tiny logos, no complex jewellery, one key accessory at most, two or three dominant outfit colours, clear left/right placement, simple readable props and stable background geometry. The less ambiguous the design, the easier it is for unrelated models to converge.

Each image prompt MUST cover all of the following inside the same prompt:

Continuity lock first: the full relevant MASTER CONTINUITY STRING, copied verbatim.

Exact story moment: who is present, what has just happened, what has not happened yet, and the precise state of the impossible rule object/symbol.

Readable body language: head direction, eye line, shoulders, hands, weight distribution, distance between characters, expression intensity and interaction with the key prop.

Fixed environment geometry: foreground object, subject plane, background anchors, door/window side, furniture placement and scale. Avoid describing the room differently from scene to scene.

Intentional framing: shot size, camera height, angle, screen direction and approximate lens language such as wide 28–35 mm equivalent, neutral 45–55 mm equivalent or compressed 75–90 mm equivalent. Use this as composition language, not photoreal camera simulation.

Lighting lock: time of day, key-light source and direction, fill level, shadow softness and palette. If the key light comes from frame left in one scene, do not casually move it to frame right in the next scene unless the location/time changes.

2D render lock: clean matte fills, simple charcoal linework, subtle two-step cel shading, restrained texture, realistic proportions, no photoreal skin, no glossy 3D material response, no painterly brushwork.

Vertical readability: 9:16 composition, important face/prop in the central safe area, clear silhouette, uncluttered top/bottom zones for subtitles or platform UI, one dominant visual idea readable at phone size.

Scene-specific negative instruction: no text/captions/logos/watermarks unless explicitly requested; no extra limbs/fingers; no duplicate character; no altered face age; no hair-length drift; no outfit recolour; no mirrored accessory; no background-layout drift; no incorrect rule state; no extra supernatural effect.

Each video prompt MUST cover all of the following inside the same prompt:

Continuity lock first: repeat the exact relevant MASTER CONTINUITY STRING verbatim, even when a matching still exists elsewhere. Assume the video model cannot see it.

Opening frame specification: exact shot size, camera height, subject screen position, pose, hand/object positions, eye line, background anchors and rule-symbol state at second zero.

One primary action only: define a simple action that can evolve cleanly over the target seconds — a hand hesitates over a button, a character turns toward a changed display, a card is slowly lowered, a person takes two steps and stops. Supporting motion must remain minor.

Timed progression: describe the motion in beginning → middle → end order. The model should know what is static, what moves and when the movement stops.

One restrained camera behaviour: locked camera, subtle push-in, slow lateral pan, tiny handheld-like drift or gentle parallax. Do not combine zoom, orbit, crane and whip pan in one micro-clip.

Persistence requirements: face shape, hairstyle, body proportions, wardrobe colours, accessory side, prop count, room geometry, lighting direction, cel-shading treatment and rule-symbol state remain unchanged unless the script explicitly changes one of them.

Stable ending frame: specify the exact final pose and composition so the editor receives a clean cut point. Avoid ending mid-step, mid-blink or during a morph.

Temporal negatives: no cuts, scene changes, morphing, face drift, age drift, hair growth, outfit changes, accessory swapping, object teleportation, extra people entering, warped hands, random text, flicker, lighting pulses, camera jumps, lip-sync, spoken dialogue, captions or watermarks.

CROSS-MODEL MATCHING PRIORITY
When image and video are generated by different models without references, prioritize matching in this order: identity silhouette → face/hair → outfit colours → key accessory → location geometry → light direction → rule-object state → line/shading style → exact pose. Exact pose is intentionally last because independent generators may differ slightly; story continuity matters more than pixel matching.

Do not create edits that demand impossible frame-perfect matching between unrelated generators. Avoid cutting directly from a still close-up to a video close-up of the exact same pose. Prefer a natural beat change, a slightly different shot scale, an insert of the rule object, or a cut after the character has logically changed pose. This hides harmless generative variation while preserving identity and world continuity.

BANNED: “Temple at sunset, cinematic light.” / “Same girl, same room, she looks scared.” / “Animate previous frame.” when no reference is actually available.

REQUIRED: full shootable specifics a generator can independently reconstruct — exact person design, exact outfit, exact room geometry, exact impossible element, exact light direction, exact framing, exact action, exact start/end state and exact locked 2D treatment.

HOOK EVERY TIME: the opening scene and selected cover frame must work as a scroll-stopper through one immediately legible contradiction, decision or emotional reaction. Prefer a strong silhouette plus one impossible element over visual clutter. No channel intros, generic greetings or abstract summaries before the hook.
